Notes: Mid-1st century BCE (midpoint -50). M. Gichon (in Stern ed., New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land, 1993), as quoted: 'In the middle of the first century BCE, Emmaus was the capital of one of the toparchies of Judea.' Basis for Year Established: earliest dating of Emmaus as a Judean (Jewish) district town; no earlier documented Jewish residents found (1 Macc mentions only Seleucid camps and garrison). No count.

43 BCE. Josephus, Antiquities 14.272-275 (14.11.2): Cassius exacted 700 talents from Judaea and 'reduced to servitude four cities, of which the most important were Gophna and Emmaus' (with Lydda and Thamna), for failing to pay their share. Shows Emmaus as one of the leading Jewish towns of Judaea; its inhabitants (no number given) were sold into slavery. Not a documented total absence (they were later freed).

c. 42/41 BCE. Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Emmaus': the inhabitants sold as slaves by Cassius were, 'through the exertions of Hyrcanus', freed by Marcus Antonius (Josephus, Ant. 14.12.2). Implies return/restoration of the Jewish townspeople; no count.

38 BCE. Josephus, War 1.319: the Roman commander Machaeras, repulsed by Antigonus, 'was forced to retire to Emmaus and rejoin Herod' and 'killed all the Jews whom he met on his march'. Herod's camp was at Emmaus; the Jews killed were met on the road and are not stated to be residents of Emmaus. Weak, indirect evidence of Jewish population in the area; no count.

Herodian period (37-4 BCE, midpoint -20). Biblical Archaeology Society caption (image from BAR 34:2, 2008, H. Shanks, 'Emmaus: Where Christ Appeared', which treats Emmaus-Nicopolis): 'JEWISH PRESENCE at Emmaus is evident in the rock-cut graves from the Herodian period that employed typical Jewish burial practices': kokhim (loculi) and secondary burial in limestone ossuaries with typical Jewish decoration. Archaeological evidence of a Jewish resident community (family tombs); no size given.

4 BCE. Josephus, War 2.63: during the revolt after Herod's death the rebel leader Athronges' band 'ventured to encompass a whole troop of Romans at Emmaus, who were carrying corn and weapons to their legion' (Gichon, NEAEHL, calls Emmaus the centre of Athronges' insurrection). Event row; Roman casualties in the attack are not population.

4 BCE. Josephus, War 2.71: 'Emmaus was also burnt, upon the flight of its inhabitants... at the command of Varus' in reprisal for the slaughter of Arius' men. Population 0 = the town was abandoned by its inhabitants and burnt at this moment; the Jewish population later returned (Emmaus is again a Judean toparchy in 66-67 CE).

Early Roman, 1st c. BCE-1st c. CE (midpoint 4, c.). BibleWalks: 'a set of ossuaries from Jewish tombs found in nearby Emmaus (1st century BC to 1st century AD)', displayed in a museum near the site. Jewish burial evidence (secondary burial in ossuaries) indicating Jewish residents; possibly the same tombs as the Herodian kokhim graves in the BAS row. No count.

Before 70 CE (Temple period; 1st c. CE midpoint 50, c.). Mishnah Arakhin 2:4: R. Yosei says the Temple musicians were Israelites from 'the family of the house of Pegarim and the family of the house of Tzippara from the city of Emaum' (Heb. ומאמאום), of lineage pure enough to marry their daughters to priests. Literary attestation of distinguished Jewish (Israelite) families living at Emmaus while the Temple stood; identification of Mishnaic Emaum with Emmaus-Nicopolis is the standard one but is not stated in the text. Number of families not given.

66 CE. Josephus, War 2.567: at the outbreak of the Great Revolt the Jerusalem rebel government sent 'John, the Essene, to the toparchy of Thamna; Lydda was also added to his portion, and Joppa, and Emmaus.' Emmaus under the Jewish revolutionary administration; no count.

c. 67 CE. Josephus, War 3.55: in his description of Judaea's districts, Emmaus is listed with Gophna, Acrabatta, Thamna and Lydda among the toparchies of Judaea. Emmaus as a Jewish district town at the time of the revolt; no count.

68 CE. M. Avi-Yonah, Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Emmaus': 'Vespasian established a fortified camp at Emmaus (in 68 c.e.) and stationed the Fifth Macedonian Legion there' (Josephus, War 4.444-445). Roman legionary garrison (troop numbers are not population); the fate of the Jewish inhabitants is not stated. EJ also says Jews continued to live in the city until 639 (later period, not used).
